mapping.what: Map this theorem; do not prove it. Turn it from prose into a graph of tasks.  A task is one step an agent can finish in one run and check by building: state the theorem in Lean with a sorry; find a lemma in Mathlib or state what is missing; prove one lemma; assemble; check the axioms. A task is never a whole theorem or a whole body of theory. If a step needs its own lemmas, break it down too.  Find the tasks that do not depend on each other. That is the point of the graph: tasks with no edge between them run at the same time, so a map that comes back as a chain wastes the engine. Most lemmas of a proof are independent of each other and depend only on the statement. Draw an edge only where one task genuinely cannot start until another is finished, and say why in the edge.  Hand back .ostoyae/report.json with: work, one item per task, a short id and one line saying exactly what to do; edges, from each task to the task that cannot start without it, with a why, so the graph reads start to finish and the last edges point at this theorem; map.settles, one or two sentences saying what a finished result is: the Lean statement, sorry-free, kernel-checked, in which file; map.cost, one of small, medium, large, unknown, small meaning one run should land the whole thing and large meaning bodies of theory are missing; map.notes, anything the agents doing the tasks should know. result.wall: Rosser's theorem (p_n > n log n) cannot be closed against Mathlib v4.33 because Mathlib has no prime number theorem, and no weaker prime-counting bound can substitute. The reduction is exact: p_n > n log n for all n >= 1 is equivalent to pi(x) * log(pi(x)) < x for all x >= 2 (proved unconditionally in lean/Frontier/Rosser.lean as `rosserStatement_iff`). Feed that any bound of shape pi(x) <= C * x / log x and it yields pi(x) * log(pi(x)) <= C*x*(1 - (log log x - log C)/log x), so the theorem needs log log x > (log x)*(C-1)/C + log C. For any fixed C > 1 the right side grows linearly in log x and the left like log log x, so it fails for all large x no matter how large a finite range is checked by hand. C must therefore be exactly 1, which is the PNT; and since the true margin is only x*(log log x - 1)/log x, a factor log log x above the second-order term of pi, what is actually consumed is PNT WITH an error term of size o(x * log log x / (log x)^2), i.e. psi(x) = x + o(x/log x). Mathlib's strongest unconditional prime-counting facts are Chebyshev's, leading constant Real.log 4 = 1.3862 (`Chebyshev.pi_le_log4_mul_div`, `Chebyshev.eventually_primeCounting_le`), and no elementary sharpening closes the gap either: the best elementary constants in the literature (Rosser-Schoenfeld psi(x) < 1.03883x, Costa Pereira 1.0353) are also > 1 and die to the same display. Mathlib has no Wiener-Ikehara / Newman Tauberian theorem and no zeta zero-free region, so there is nothing in tree to build the C = 1 bound from. What did land, sorry-free and kernel-checked (axioms exactly [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]): lean/Frontier/Rosser.lean with the statement `RosserStatement`, the exact reduction `rosserStatement_iff`, and Rosser up to a constant - `mul_log_le_const_mul_nth_prime`: n*log n <= (2*log 4 + 1)*p_n unconditionally, `mul_log_lt_four_mul_nth_prime`: n*log n < 4*p_n, and `eventually_mul_log_lt_nth_prime`: for every eps > 0, eventually n*log n <= (log 4 + eps)*p_n, which is the best constant reachable from Mathlib today. The distance left to travel is exactly log 4 -> 1.

attempts.what: Prove the Erdos-Kac theorem in Lean 4 against mathlib, sorry-free, in lean/Frontier/ErdosKac.lean. mathlib docs/1000.yaml has no decl for it.

result.wall: Erdos-Kac is not one missing lemma, it is two missing bodies of theory, and I could close neither in this cell. (1) Probabilistic side: Mathlib v4.33.0-rc2 has the i.i.d. central limit theorem (ProbabilityTheory.tendstoInDistribution_inv_sqrt_mul_sum_sub) and the Levy continuity theorem, but no Lindeberg-Feller theorem for triangular arrays of independent non-identically-distributed variables, no method of moments (convergence of all moments to the Gaussian ones implies convergence in distribution), and not even the Gaussian moments themselves: a grep of Mathlib/Probability and Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Gaussian finds no statement of int x^(2m) dgaussianReal 0 1 = (2m-1)!!. Without one of those two the arithmetic moments cannot be turned into a distributional limit at all. (2) Arithmetic side: the exact k-th moment identity I did prove here (sum_omega_pow_eq: sum_{n<=N} omega(n)^k = sum over k-tuples s of primes <= N of floor(N / prod(range s))) is unusable as it stands, because replacing each floor(N/d) by N/d costs O(1) per tuple and there are pi(N)^k tuples, which swamps N. The standard fix is to truncate: work with omega_z(n) = #{p <= z : p | n} for z = N^(1/s), where omega(n) - omega_z(n) <= s pointwise, so the error becomes O(z^k) = o(N). There is no truncated omega in this tree and no comparison lemma for it, and past that point the moment evaluation needs Mertens' second theorem raised to the k-th power with the diagonal terms controlled uniformly in k. Each of those is a piece of work in its own right, not a step. What I did close is the combinatorial entry point, sorry-free and kernel-checked: the statement, the exact k-th moment identity in three forms (tuple, grouped by the set of primes with surjection weights, and split into injective and diagonal tuples). The k=1 case is rederived from the general identity as a check that the statement is the right one.
